title: The heap's fire kept through the three-day gale
summary: A winter gale tears the roof from the shelter behind the shell heap at Dunn and drives the sea over the gathering-rocks for three days; the fire kept at the heap's foot is banked low and fed through the storm by whoever can be spared, and does not go out.

title: The gatherer's mother dies at the tide
summary: An old woman of the Dunn heap, who has worked the shore pools long past when her hands were fit for it, is found sitting against a rock with the tide turning round her feet, dead as quietly as she lived; what is done with her is not carried past the household's own places.

title: A season worked alone at the heap
summary: Through the season after her mother's death the gatherer works the shore pools alone, going down before light and coming up after dark, and keeps the heap's fire no lower than it was kept with two pairs of hands, before her own daughter is old enough to work beside her.

title: An old scraper turned up in the heap
summary: Loosening an old shoulder of the Dunn heap, a girl finds a flint scraper struck and finished unlike any tool freshly made at the heap's fire that same season; she turns it over a while and lets it fall back into the shell with everything else the heap has taken in.

title: The heap first used to watch the sea
summary: A boy sent to fetch fire down for the smoking of fish remarks, standing at the heap's foot, that its top gives the farthest view of the water on that stretch of coast; after that day the heap is climbed from time to time to watch for boats or weather.

title: The Dunn heap stands a man's height
summary: The shell heap above the shore at Dunn, built shell by shell and bag by bag over more lifetimes than any one gatherer can reckon, now stands higher at its crown than a grown man can reach with his arm raised, the tallest thing on that shore.

title: The net-maker of Cwen begins the long mesh
summary: At Cwen, on the sheltered bay to the south, a net-maker who has always set short nets from each shallow toward an open channel begins, over a winter's close work by the fire, twisting a mesh long enough to close the whole width of the bay's mouth.

title: The Cwen nets first set across the bay
summary: The net-maker's household stakes a single unbroken net from shallow to shallow across the mouth of the bay at Cwen for the first time, the net-maker herself wading the deepest channel to sink the centre true; more fish come against it than the smoking-racks can hold.

title: Households come to see the closed net
summary: Word of the catch taken at the closed net travels the shore, and households from some way off come to see the long line of stakes and weights for themselves, going home to lengthen their own nets by whatever means each knows.

title: The net-maker's daughter learns the groove
summary: The net-maker's daughter, grown old enough for close work, begins sitting beside her mother through whole afternoons at the stone weights, learning by eye alone which beach stones will split true under the pecking and which will shatter wrong.

title: The daughter's first spoiled stones
summary: Given a stone and the small flint used for the cutting, the net-maker's daughter is set to notching the three strokes; her first attempts run too long, too short or crossing, and each spoiled stone goes back to the unworked pile without comment.

title: The daughter cuts the three strokes true
summary: On a calm morning the net-maker's daughter cuts three strokes into a finished weight and finds nothing in it her trained eye can fault; her mother takes it up, turns it in the same light, and sets down the next stone before her without a word.
